5ebffa8225:
This chapter is a first-principles look at the work that comes before and after the code of an LLM feature. It covers four things:

  • turning a business ask into requirements a probabilistic system can be held to;
  • writing success criteria as evals before writing prompts;
  • stating the non-functional requirements (latency, cost, safety, data handling) that pick the model, the API mode and the platform;
  • running the life cycle from prototype through evaluation, pilot, production, monitoring and iteration.

Model deprecation and upgrade get treated as a scheduled life-cycle event, not a surprise. The story runs from requirements engineering and CRISP-DM to eval-driven development. Implementations are in Python and Java.
6a50acaf27: Neighbouring chapters: chapter 01 picks the pattern (workflow or agent) once requirements are known. Chapter 07 covers the Batch API that many requirements point to. Chapter 10 owns the mechanics of model pinning, prompt versioning and settings files. Chapter 12 owns debugging and error recovery. Chapter 15 owns model trade-offs and cost mechanics. This chapter decides what must be true and how you keep it true.
1f1257e390:
An LLM feature is not specified until you have said how often it must be right, per kind of input, what a wrong answer costs, who or what consumes the output, and what latency, cost, safety and data-handling limits it must live inside; and the only honest way to write "how often it must be right" is as an evaluation that exists before the first prompt does.

The life cycle that follows is a loop, not a line: prototype against the eval, gate every change (prompt, tool, model, parameter) on it, pilot, monitor production, turn failures into new eval cases, and treat a model upgrade or retirement as one more change that must pass the same gate.
4634a91bd8:
Those two sentences carry most of the exam reasoning for objectives 2.1 and 2.2. The official guide lists them as "Understanding Requirements" (3.4%) and "Systems Life Cycle" (2.8%). Expect three or four questions that test them directly.

The concepts leak into many more. Scenario stems across Domain 2 and Domain 5 open with a business ask ("a retailer wants...", "a carrier's care team needs...") and hide a requirement in the wording:

  • "overnight" is a latency requirement that unlocks the Batch API;
  • "several applications" is a reuse requirement that points to an MCP server;
  • "must stay in our AWS account" is a data-handling requirement that points to Amazon Bedrock;
  • "issues refunds" is a wrong-answer-cost requirement that points to a human approval step.

Reading those requirements out of the stem is half of answering the question.
ea735fd4cc:
The other half is life-cycle order. Many wrong options in this area do the right thing at the wrong time. They launch and then gather feedback before any evaluation exists. They upgrade the model ID because the new model is "better", without re-running the eval. They tune the prompt on the one example a manager complained about, without adding that example to a regression set.

The correct option is almost always the one that measures first, gates on the measurement, and feeds production back into the measurement.
d6aaa6e8c3: None of this is new to an enterprise architect. Requirements and life cycles are old ground. What is new is a component whose output is a distribution rather than a value. Tracing where the existing disciplines came from shows which habits carry over unchanged, and which need an extra step.
730e1452c8:
Royce's 1970 paper is usually cited as the origin of the waterfall, though it actually argued for iteration. IEEE 830 (1998) standardised the software requirements specification. Functional requirements say what the system does. Non-functional requirements (performance, reliability, security, maintainability) say how well. And each requirement must be verifiable: there has to be a finite, cost-effective process to check that the system meets it.

That word, verifiable, is the bridge to this chapter. "The summary shall be accurate" was never a valid IEEE 830 requirement, and it isn't a valid LLM requirement either. The difference is that for an LLM the cost-effective check is statistical. It's a pass rate on a labelled set, not a single test.
49dc9de4e2:
Agile replaced the big specification with user stories plus acceptance criteria. Test-driven development made the tests the executable form of those criteria: write the failing test, make it pass, refactor. Behaviour-driven development (Given/When/Then) tried to make the criteria readable by the business owner.

The principle is to write the check before the code, so that "done" has a definition. That is exactly what Anthropic's guidance asks for with prompts: define success criteria and build the evaluation before iterating on the prompt. The adaptation is that one LLM test case is a sample, not a proof. So the "test" becomes a set of cases with a threshold.
cf33685a9b:
Data mining, and later machine learning, had to solve the probabilistic-output problem first. CRISP-DM (1996 to 2000) described a cycle of business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modelling, evaluation and deployment. It was drawn as a loop, because deployment produces new data and new questions. Its first phase, business understanding, required stating business success criteria and translating them into data-mining success criteria, such as a lift or an accuracy on a held-out set.

Google's 2015 paper "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems" (Sculley et al.) then showed that the model is a small box in a large system. Most production failures come from the surroundings: data dependencies, feedback loops, configuration, monitoring gaps. MLOps grew out of that paper.

LLM systems inherit both lessons. Business criteria must become measurable model criteria. And the hard part is everything around the model.
1c6b3d5227:
With hosted foundation models, teams no longer train the model. The ML life cycle's training stages disappear, and the remaining loop speeds up enormously: change a prompt and you have a new "model" in seconds. That speed is the risk. Early LLM products were tuned by "vibe checks" on a few favourite examples, and they regressed silently on everything else.

Anthropic's documentation responded with a sequence that the exam follows:

  1. define success criteria (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant);
  2. develop test cases that reflect real input distributions, including edge cases;
  3. choose graders: code-based where possible, LLM-based with a clear rubric where needed, human for calibration;
  4. only then iterate on the prompt.

In parallel, model providers began publishing deprecation schedules. "The model under your feature will be retired" became a predictable life-cycle event rather than an outage. Section 16 covers it.
52a567fda7:
Now consider "Given a customer's message about their bill, explain the change in plain language." The same input can produce different wording on each call. Most outputs are fine. Some are slightly off. A few are wrong in a way that matters, such as a fee described as a one-time charge when it recurs.

Changing the prompt to fix one case can quietly break another. And the inputs are open-ended: customers will ask things the designer never imagined. That gives LLM requirements three properties a conventional requirement doesn't have.
0516786110: They are rates, not booleans. The meaningful statement is "at least 95% of explanations correctly identify the cause of the change, on each of the five bill-change categories". That is a threshold on a measured proportion over a defined set of inputs.
b925da9dd1: They must say what happens when the system is wrong. Some error rate is guaranteed, so the requirement must cover the error path. Does a human review? Does low confidence route elsewhere? Can the customer reach an agent? Is the action reversible?
acb7407a0b: They are tied to an input distribution. "95% accurate" means nothing without "on what". The eval set defines the "what". That's why it is written with the requirements and versioned with them.
636197f25b:
There is a fourth, practical difference that architects underestimate. In a conventional system the behaviour lives in code, which is reviewed and tested. In an LLM system the behaviour also lives in text artefacts: the system prompt, the tool descriptions, the few-shot examples, the output schema, and the model ID and its parameters. A one-word change in a tool description can change which tool gets called.

So requirements extend to change control over those artefacts. Chapter 10 covers the mechanics of versioning and pinning them. The life cycle in the second half of this chapter exists to keep the rate-based requirements true while all of those artefacts, the inputs and the model itself keep changing.
ee4034d0a4:
Business owners rarely arrive with requirements. They arrive with an outcome ("reduce average handle time in care by 20%") or a solution ("we want a chatbot"). Elicitation is the work of turning either one into something you can build and test.

For LLM features the interview has a fixed shape, because the same ten answers decide nearly every architecture decision. Ask them in this order, in the room. Write the answers down as a versioned file, not a slide.
2fe694f48c:
Start with the task and the consumer. What exactly goes in, what exactly comes out, and who or what reads it? "Summarise the call" becomes "from a 10 to 40 minute care call transcript, produce a JSON object with a three-sentence summary, the affected site IDs and one of four next actions, read by the CRM API and shown to the next agent".

The consumer matters more than people expect. A human reader tolerates prose and minor variation. A downstream API needs a schema and validation (chapter 18).

Then ask for examples: ten real inputs with the output an expert would want. Examples are the most precise requirement you will ever get. They expose disagreements between stakeholders early ("no, port-in calls should always escalate"). And they become the seed of the eval set.
b882d04200:
Next, the error path. Ask "what happens when it is wrong?" and keep asking until the answer is concrete. A misrouted ticket that an agent re-routes in thirty seconds is cheap. A credit issued to the wrong account is expensive. So is a regulatory filing with a wrong number, or a technician sent to the wrong tower.

The answer sets the accuracy threshold. It decides whether a human approves outputs before they take effect, and whether low-confidence cases go to a person.

It also often reveals an asymmetry. In a returns-triage feature, a false "restock" (damaged goods back on the shelf) is far worse than a false "refurbish". The requirement should set a high precision on "restock" specifically, not a single accuracy number.
7b8a02ab15:
Then the non-functional limits (sections 08 and 09 go deeper). Is a person waiting, and how long can they wait? How many requests per day, and on what budget? What data is involved, and where must it be processed and stored? How trusted is the input?

Finally, reuse and ownership. Will other applications need the same capability? Who owns the feature after launch? An LLM feature with no owner for its eval set decays, because nobody adds the new failure cases.
3cc6936f84:
Writing the card as data has two benefits. It can be validated: a realtime feature without a latency target is an incomplete card. And it can drive configuration and the release gate, so the answers don't drift away from the system.

The companion's card is a dataclass with enumerated values and a problems() method. The YAML form is shown here because it's what a team would review in a pull request.
5e5fcc8f06:
Before looking at the options, write the card in your head: waiting or not, latency, volume and budget, reasoning difficulty, live data, reuse, input trust, consumer, cost of error, residency. Most stems fill two or three slots explicitly.

The correct option satisfies all the filled slots. Distractors usually satisfy one and violate another. Think of a cheaper model that still runs synchronously when "overnight" allowed batch, or an agent when the steps are fixed. Companion example 03_signal_words.py encodes the common signal phrases.
b32bc7b733: Functional requirements for a model-backed feature cover five things. The exam tends to test the last two, because they are the ones teams forget.
3dd5cb33e7: Input contract. What arrives, from where, how large, in what language, with what attachments (images, PDFs), and how trusted. Size matters because it decides context-window use and cost. Trust decides whether the input must be delimited and treated as data (chapter 19).
a4176116de: Output contract. Format (prose, JSON with a schema, a label from an enum), length bounds, and the consumer. If the consumer is code, the requirement includes validation, and what happens when validation fails.
874243f456: Scope and abstention. What the feature must not do. A bill explainer must not promise credits; a returns triage must not give legal advice. The permitted "I do not know" matters just as much: an enum value unclear, an escalate action, or a confidence field that routes to a person. Without an abstention path, the feature will produce a confident wrong answer instead, because the output contract left it no alternative.
0ccf8ce5e7: Golden examples. A small set of input/output pairs agreed with the business owner. They are a requirement (this is what good looks like) and also the first eval cases. When stakeholders disagree about an example, you have found a requirement gap. It is far cheaper to find it here than in production.
fb80196441:
Two common failures sit at this level.

The first is the solution-shaped requirement: "we need an agent that can use our CRM". An agent is a design choice, not a requirement. The requirement is the task the agent would perform, and chapter 01 shows that most such tasks are better served by a workflow.

The second is the missing negative requirement. Teams specify what the feature should do and forget what it must refuse to do. Then they discover in a pilot that the bill explainer happily offers a goodwill credit because a customer asked nicely. Write the negatives down, and write eval cases that try to trigger them.
a619d53f48:
A success criterion is the verifiable form of "how often must it be right". Anthropic's prompt-engineering documentation asks for criteria that are:

  • specific: a defined metric, not "good";
  • measurable: a number you can compute;
  • achievable: grounded in what current models and your data allow, often checked against a baseline or human performance;
  • relevant: tied to the business outcome.

It also asks for them to be multidimensional. Most features need an accuracy criterion, a safety or policy criterion, and latency and cost criteria together, because optimising one alone moves the others.
4889d46736:
Every criterion needs four parts: a metric (what is computed), a threshold (the pass line), a grader (who or what computes it) and a dataset (on which inputs). Remove any one and the criterion can't be checked.

"Accurate summaries" has none of them. "Tone acceptable" has a metric but no grader. "95% accuracy" has a threshold but no dataset, so nobody can reproduce it next month.
d604737093:
Eval-first means the criteria and the eval set exist before the prompt is iterated. The reason is the same as for test-first development, and non-determinism makes it stronger.

Without an eval, you judge prompt changes by reading a few outputs. Human reading is biased toward the cases you just fixed. With an eval, you see the whole distribution after every change. Say the fix for port-in calls dropped roaming accuracy by six points. You see that immediately, not in a customer complaint three weeks later.

Eval-first also forces the stakeholder conversation early. Labelling 200 real cases makes people disagree about what "correct" means. Every such disagreement is a requirement that was missing.
c7f196b5ab:
Grade with code whenever code can decide: exact label match, JSON validity, schema and enum conformance, presence of required fields, a regex for leaked identifiers, a numeric tolerance on an extracted total. Code graders are fast, free and deterministic, so they can run on every pull request.

Use an LLM judge for qualities code can't check: faithfulness to a source, tone, whether a summary would help a field technician. Give it a written rubric and a constrained output (PASS/FAIL, or a 1-5 score with a reason). Ideally give it a different prompt context from the generator. A model reviewing its own output in the same context tends to approve it.

Use human grading for the most subjective criteria. Above all, use it to calibrate the LLM judge. Score a sample by hand and compare. Only trust the judge as a gate when agreement is high and it doesn't pass cases humans fail.
57f2c63cf4:
The output shows a common trap. 93% raw agreement sounds good. But kappa (agreement corrected for chance) is only 0.54, and the judge is lenient: it passes three summaries that humans failed. As a release gate it would let regressions through.

The fix is a tighter rubric with examples of failing summaries, then re-calibration. Only after that should the judge's score be allowed to block or permit a merge.
44a37ecb9d: The eval set is the operational definition of the requirement. Its quality caps the quality of every decision made with it. Three properties matter. It must look like production. It must cover the cases that matter, even when they are rare. And it must be big enough that a difference you care about is not noise.
5307f3bd6c:
Looks like production. Draw cases from real inputs, redacted as your data-handling requirements demand. Don't rely on what an engineer imagines customers say. Synthetic cases are useful to fill gaps, especially adversarial ones. But a set made only of synthetic cases measures the engineer's imagination.

Label with the people whose judgement defines "correct": experienced agents, analysts, compliance staff. Write the labelling guideline down. It is the requirement in its most precise form.
b8abd4dd5b:
Covers what matters. A random sample mirrors traffic, so rare segments get a handful of cases or none. If a requirement is stated per segment (per contract type, per language, per product category), the eval set must be stratified. That means a minimum number of cases in each segment, however rare the segment is in traffic.

Add explicit slices for edge cases: two issues in one message, very long inputs, missing fields. Add adversarial cases too: prompt-injection attempts in a customer email, requests that should be refused, inputs containing PII that must not be echoed.
776fe363a1:
Big enough. A pass rate measured on n cases has an uncertainty, and with small n it is large. The companion's Wilson-interval calculation shows the effect. 22 correct out of 25 is 88%, but the 95% interval runs from 70% to 96%. So 25 cases can't tell an 88% feature from a 95% one. At 400 cases the same 88% has an interval of 84% to 91%.

Detecting a 5-point improvement from 90% to 95% between two prompt versions needs roughly 430 cases per variant, at conventional significance and power. Detecting 93% versus 95% needs over 2,000.

The practical rules:

  • use at least 50 to 100 cases per segment for a gate, and more where the threshold is tight;
  • treat differences smaller than the interval as no difference;
  • when a segment is too small to measure, say so in the gate output instead of reporting a precise-looking number.
eb40a0ce1e: Finally, version the eval set like code. Keep a held-out portion that prompt authors don't look at while iterating. If the same 200 cases are used for every tweak, the prompt slowly overfits to them, and the eval score stops predicting production quality. The held-out set is what the release gate runs. The development set is what you iterate against.
d2b00ac3ed: Non-functional requirements decide the model, the API mode and much of the architecture, often more than the functional ones do. For LLM features they need sharper definitions than "fast" and "cheap". The components of latency and cost behave differently from a REST service.
560be85b81:
End-to-end time for a model call is roughly three parts added together: network and queueing overhead, time to first token (TTFT, dominated by processing the input), and output tokens divided by output speed. Extended thinking adds thinking tokens to the output side, and they are generated before the visible answer.

Which number the requirement constrains depends on the consumer. A person reading a chat answer experiences TTFT if you stream, because text appears as it is generated. Streaming doesn't make the call faster. It makes the wait visible sooner. A handheld app that needs a parsed JSON decision experiences the total time, because it can't act on half an object. A batch job experiences neither, only the completion window.

So a latency requirement must name three things: the metric (TTFT or total), the percentile (p95, not average, because the tail is what users notice), and the load at which it holds.
9dbe3ac9d5:
The arithmetic is deliberately simple. The speeds in the companion are placeholders, not published figures. Real numbers come from your own load test against the model and region you will use.

The point is the shape. A 3-second total budget for a 120-token JSON decision rules out the largest tier at these assumptions, before any quality comparison. A streamed chat answer with a 1.5-second first-text target is met comfortably by the two smaller tiers. Adding a few thousand thinking tokens blows any interactive budget. That's why extended thinking and high effort settings are usually requirements-driven choices for offline or analyst-facing work (chapter 13 covers the mechanics).
603b768ed5:
Volume becomes a requirement twice: as cost, and as throughput against rate limits. The API enforces limits per organisation and model, on requests per minute and on input and output tokens per minute (check the docs for your tier's values). Overload returns errors that clients must retry with backoff (chapter 12).

A requirement of "180,000 summaries per day" is about two per second on average. But care traffic peaks. If 30% arrives in two hours, the peak is several times the average, and the token-per-minute limit for long transcripts is often the binding constraint. State the peak, not just the daily total. Check it against the limits during design, not at launch.
a391654703:
Cost is input tokens times input price, plus output tokens times output price, times volume. Two mechanisms change the input side a great deal.

Prompt caching charges cached prefix reads at a fraction of the normal input price, and cache writes at a premium. A long, stable system prompt plus tool definitions becomes cheap after the first call. Chapter 15 covers the mechanics.

The Message Batches API charges about half price for work that can wait up to 24 hours (chapter 07).

The requirement should state a cost ceiling per request or per month, and the assumptions behind it.
82200987f3:
Read the table as a requirements conversation, not a price list. Suppose the business case needs the feature under $30,000 a month at this volume. Then the Sonnet-without-caching design is out, whatever its quality. The question becomes whether Haiku meets the accuracy criteria on the eval set. If the summaries are only read the next morning, batch halves the bill with no quality change at all.

The eval set decides quality. The cost model decides which candidates are worth evaluating.
070589e34e: The second group of non-functional requirements is about harm. It splits into three parts: what the model might say, what it might do, and what happens to the data that passes through it. Each has a different owner in an enterprise (product, security, privacy and legal). Each must be in the requirements card before design starts, because retrofitting them changes the architecture.
7af97d175d:
Two habits help.

First, data minimisation as a requirement. If the task is "explain why the bill went up", the model needs the line items, not the customer's date of birth or full card number. Removing fields before the call is cheaper and more reliable than telling the model not to repeat them.

Second, safety criteria are absolute where possible: "zero full phone numbers in outputs on the adversarial slice", not "99% of outputs contain no phone number". Absolute criteria belong in the release gate as hard failures, independent of the accuracy thresholds. Then a version that is more accurate but leaks once can't ship.

Chapters 19 and 20 cover the controls. This chapter's job is to make sure the requirement exists and is tested.
8a88e62345: With the card filled in, most architecture decisions follow mechanically. The ones that don't are the ones that need an experiment. The companion's derive() function encodes the mapping, so you can test your reasoning against it. More usefully, you can see which decisions move when a requirement changes.
a264f73590:
Notice that the function produces a starting model, not a final one. Model tier is the one decision a lookup table can't make. The right answer depends on how the candidates score on your eval set, at your latency and cost limits. The requirements narrow the candidates; the eval picks among them.

That ordering matters on the exam. Watch for an option that picks the largest model "for best accuracy" without reference to the latency or cost requirement. Or one that picks the smallest "to save money" without reference to the accuracy criterion. Both are usually distractors. Chapter 15 covers tier trade-offs in detail.
4492ad9e7e:
The stages are the ones you already know: requirements, design, build, test, deploy, operate. But three facts about LLM systems change how they connect.

  • Behaviour lives in text artefacts as well as code, so a prompt edit, a tool description change or a model ID change is a release.
  • Tests are statistical, so the test stage is an eval run with per-segment thresholds rather than a green bar.
  • And inputs and models drift. Customers start asking about a new device, a provider retires the model you pinned, and quality changes with no commit on your side.

The result is a life cycle with two loops sharing one artefact.
f8bf715324:
The inner loop runs during development. Change one thing, run the eval, read the failures, change the next thing. It runs in minutes, and it's where the prompt, tool descriptions and output contract get shaped.

The outer loop runs after launch. Monitor production, sample and label outputs, and find the new failure modes. Add them as eval cases, fix them in the inner loop, and release through the gate.

The eval set is the contract between the loops. It grows with every production failure, so the feature can only regress on a case once.
27918d0015: Each stage has an exit criterion. The commonest life-cycle failure is skipping one, usually going from "the prototype looks good on 15 examples" straight to production. The companion models the stages as a state machine that refuses to advance when an exit criterion is unmet. That's a useful mental model even if your process lives in a ticketing system rather than code.
3c660aa0db:
The prototype stage deserves a word, because it's where teams over-invest. Its job is to show feasibility, not to produce the final prompt. A prototype that answers ten typical inputs well proves the task is within reach. It says nothing about the 5% of inputs that will generate complaints.

Stop polishing and build the eval set as soon as feasibility is clear. Every hour of prompt work before the eval exists is tuned to the examples you happened to look at.
0f92963e4e:
The harden stage is ordinary engineering, and an architect's existing instincts apply:

  • timeouts;
  • retries with backoff for overload and rate-limit errors;
  • idempotency for actions;
  • circuit breakers or a degraded mode;
  • validation of model output before it reaches a consumer;
  • limits on spend.

Chapter 12 covers these as error-handling and debugging technique, and chapter 18 covers output handling. The life-cycle point is that hardening is an explicit stage with an exit test, not something added after the first incident.
7594038cea:
The heart of the life cycle is a small program. It runs a candidate configuration (prompt version, tool definitions, model ID, parameters) over the eval set. It grades every case, reports per segment, and exits non-zero if any criterion fails. In CI, that exit code blocks the merge.

The companion's harness runs two prompt versions over the same 100 cases. Its fake model confuses roaming tickets under v1.0, and the per-segment view makes that regression visible.
03c2dba742: For a real run, the harness shouldn't call the API synchronously case by case. Eval runs are not latency-sensitive, so the Message Batches API fits them well (chapter 07). Submit all cases with custom_id set to the case ID, poll until processing ends, then join results back by ID. That halves the cost of every eval run, which matters when the gate runs on every pull request.
64dc14cbd2:
The most frequent gate mistake is averaging. Take a contract-review assistant that must reach 95% on each contract type. It can show 97.2% overall while one type sits at 86.7%, because the large segments dominate the average.

The second mistake is treating a safety limit as one more percentage, so a single leaked identifier gets averaged away. The third is reporting a precise number for a segment too small to support it.
c4488bcaae: In CI the gate triggers on every path that changes behaviour. That's wider than a Spring team's habit of testing on changes to src/. Prompt files, tool definitions, the model configuration and the eval set itself are all behaviour-changing artefacts. Chapter 10 covers how those artefacts are versioned and pinned. The point here is only that each of them runs the same gate.
75c1213631: Passing the eval proves the feature meets the criteria on the eval distribution. The pilot proves the eval distribution resembles production. The two most useful pilot designs come straight from conventional release engineering.
c89b8c62d5:
In shadow mode the model runs on real traffic, but its output isn't used. The human (or the old system) still decides, and disagreements are logged and labelled. Shadow mode is ideal when the cost of a wrong answer is high. It measures production quality at zero customer risk, and the labelled disagreements are exactly the new eval cases you need.

In a canary the model's output is used for a small share of traffic: 1%, then 5%, then 25%. At each step, live metrics are compared against limits, with automatic rollback to the pinned baseline if a limit is breached. Canaries catch what shadow mode can't: the effect of the output on user behaviour, such as more repeat contacts or more escalations.
7a3f0ad3db:
Rollback is only possible if the baseline still exists. That ties the pilot to configuration management: the previous prompt version and the previous pinned model ID must be deployable at the flip of a flag (chapter 10).

It also ties to model retirement. You can't roll back to a model that has been retired. That's one reason to migrate well before a retirement date, not in the final week.
94e9bc5c18:
Once live, the system must answer three questions for any request:

  • what exactly was sent (prompt version, model ID, tool set, parameters);
  • what came back (content, stop_reason, tool calls);
  • what it cost (the usage block, including cache reads and writes).

Log a structured record per call, and redact personal data in the record. If investigators may need the raw input later, keep a hash of the input plus a pointer to a secure store.
8f2af641c6:
Metrics from those records give early warning. Sampled, labelled outputs give the truth. The table lists the signals that most often move, and what they usually mean.

Diagnosing a specific failure (is it the integration layer or the model output?) is chapter 12's subject. Monitoring's job is to notice that something moved, and to route samples into the outer loop.
d9ee869f7c:
Input drift is the silent killer of LLM features. Nothing changes in your repository, yet quality falls, because customers began asking about something the eval set never contained.

The companion measures it two ways. The population stability index compares this week's segment mix with the baseline; a value above about 0.25 is conventionally a major shift. Per-segment sampled quality then shows where the damage is.

In the example, a new esim_transfer segment has appeared at 20% of traffic, with sampled quality of 61%. Every known segment is fine. The overall average would hide it for weeks.
70d0e31014: Iteration closes the loop. Every production failure that someone reports, and every sampled failure, becomes an eval case with a label. Then the gate catches the same failure if it ever returns. Teams that fix the reported case by editing the prompt and stop there tend to fix it again three months later.
770267e10b:
Everything above assumes the model under the feature stays the same. It doesn't. New models arrive with better quality or lower prices, and old ones are retired. Anthropic's model deprecations page defines the stages a model passes through:

  • Active: fully supported and recommended.
  • Legacy: no longer receives updates, and may be deprecated in the future.
  • Deprecated: still functional but no longer recommended. Anthropic names a recommended replacement and assigns a retirement date.
  • Retired: no longer available. Requests fail.

For publicly released models, Anthropic states it gives at least 60 days' notice before retirement to customers with active deployments, by email and in the documentation. The page also notes that partner-operated platforms (Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud) set their own retirement schedules, so dates can differ by platform.

These facts were read from the deprecations page in October 2026. Check the docs for current wording and dates.
b3a2e64835:
From the life-cycle point of view there are two kinds of model change. A voluntary upgrade is a decision. A new model may be cheaper, faster or more accurate, and you choose whether and when to move. A forced migration is scheduled by the provider: the model you pinned will stop answering on a known date. Both go through the same gate. The forced one has a deadline.

Treat retirement dates as dependencies, the way you'd treat an end-of-life Java version or a vendor API sunset. Track them in the inventory of features and assign an owner. Plan the migration with enough time for the full gate, a canary and a possible second iteration.
0bf66003b5:
What changes between models is rarely just accuracy. New models can format output differently and follow instructions more literally. They can refuse in different places, call tools more or less eagerly, and use more or fewer tokens for the same task. They can support different parameters.

Release notes and migration guides list known breaking changes: removed or renamed parameters, changed defaults, new behaviours such as different thinking options. Read them before the eval run, so you know which slices to watch.

Chapter 15 covers model trade-offs and breaking changes in detail. Chapter 10 covers the pinning mechanics: dated snapshot IDs versus aliases that move, and where the model ID lives in configuration.
0d3c0a8970:
The output shows why the deadline matters. The candidate is better overall and on two of three segments. But it regresses on roaming, and it more than doubles refusals.

That's a normal result, not a failure of the new model. Prompts are tuned to the model they were developed on, and a migration usually needs a round of prompt iteration. With 53 days left, there is time for one iteration and a canary, and not much more. Teams that started at the deprecation announcement have months. Teams that started at the reminder email have weeks.
95236643aa:
Two operational habits complete the picture.

Keep an inventory of every feature: the model ID it pins, the platform it runs on, and the eval set and owner that go with it. Then a deprecation notice becomes a list of tickets rather than a search.

And use the provider's usage reporting to find unexpected callers of a retiring model. The deprecations page points to the Console usage export, which breaks usage down by API key and model (check the docs for the current location).
2fcda8695d:
If your team runs Spring services, the requirements card and the eval gate fit the existing build with little ceremony. Bind the card to a typed configuration class, so the service and the gate read the same numbers. Run the eval as a separate Gradle or Maven test source set that executes only when behaviour-changing files change.

The model call goes through the Anthropic Java SDK, or your internal gateway, behind an interface. That way the same gate can run against a fake in unit tests and against the real model in the eval job.
dba0252ddd:
Keep the threshold logic in one place (the card), so the Python and Java gates can't disagree. Keep the gate in its own source set, so ordinary unit tests stay fast and free.

The same structure supports the upgrade gate from section 16. Parameterise the test with the model ID from configuration and run it twice: once for the pinned baseline, once for the candidate. Then compare the two reports.
325140c450: CCDV-F items give a short scenario and four options. For 2.1 and 2.2, the wrong options are usually sensible activities in the wrong order, or measurements at the wrong granularity. Work each one before reading the reasoning.
0b0b770e91: Fifteen hand-reviewed outputs are a feasibility check, not evidence. B is the eval-first sequence: criteria, a representative stratified set, measurement, then a pilot. A puts measurement after harm. C picks a model without any criterion or measurement, and may break latency or cost limits. D is premature, and 15 examples are far too few.
d934078321:
The card says: nobody waits (results are read next morning), high volume, cost-sensitive. That's the Batch API case, at about half price, with the model tier chosen by eval.

A pays realtime prices and the largest model, with no latency requirement to justify it. C adds autonomy and cost the summarisation task doesn't need. D keeps the realtime price, risks rate limits on 2 million calls in an hour, and leaves no margin before 8 a.m.
f00c094067: The requirement is stated per contract type, so the gate must be per type. An average dominated by large segments hides a failing small one. A and B ship a known failure. D hides it by changing the measurement instead of the system. If 60 cases were too few to trust, the answer would be to add cases, not to remove the segment.
73dbb05311: Public benchmarks don't measure your task on your distribution. B is the life-cycle answer: a model change is a behaviour change, and it goes through the same per-segment gate and canary. A makes the problem automatic. C and D are guesses that measure nothing.
bc41cd211f: Retirement is a scheduled life-cycle event with a deadline: requests to retired models fail. B finds every dependency, assigns ownership, and starts the same gate early enough to iterate. A leaves no room for a failed canary or rollback. C is not a plan. D skips evaluation, and may break latency and cost requirements.
b3da347dd8: This is input drift: the distribution changed, not the system. The outer loop turns the new failures into eval cases. The fix is measured, and the regression can't recur unseen. A rolls back to a version that never saw the new input either. C and D are unmeasured guesses, and D may break latency and cost requirements.
9119bb777b: "Who consumes the output" is one of the requirements that changes the design most. A machine consumer needs a schema, validation and a defined abstention path. The error cost (a day of delay) sets per-label accuracy targets. A ignores all this. C makes parsing harder. D adds autonomy where the task is a classification.
eb2eb3d18f: In 01_requirements_card.py, write the card for a nightly alarm-summary job: 2 million alarms per day, read at 8 a.m., cost-sensitive. Run 02_derive_architecture.py on it, and list which decisions differ from the care-summary card.
54f3b25fd9: Done when: you can turn any business ask into a ten-answer card in five minutes. You can write a criterion with metric, threshold, grader and dataset for each requirement. You can explain why the gate is per segment and has absolute safety limits. And you can describe the migration plan for a deprecated model without looking at notes.
